children: Countries are reaching a breaking point in their efforts to shield people from energy and food price hikes, the UN Development Program has warned, with global fuel subsidies potentially surpassing $1T this year.
The Iran war and the resulting energy shock have pushed governments around the world to announce subsidies, price caps and rationing to shield their populations from higher prices.

To continue these policy interventions, many governments require additional fiscal resources as the war drags on. "This exacerbates the debt-development trade-off, which in many – especially poorer – countries diminishes long-term development prospects," the UNDP noted.

The agency flagged other compounding economic shocks – a super El Niño, increased bond volatility, and constraints in four trade corridors at once (the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, the Black Sea and the Panama Canal).
"These effects extend far beyond the Middle East region through energy, food, fertilizer, transport, trade, and volatility in financial markets," the UNDP stated.
In turn, these factors create a broad shock-management challenge for developing countries already struggling with limited fiscal space, high debt, inflationary pressures and import dependence.

title: Countries running out of room to cushion energy shock impact, UNDP warns
